findings.title: `pipeline.background_idle_timeout_s` is read from the session's cwd, not the pipeline's cwd
findings.description: `_background_idle_timeout_s()` derives the config directory from `self.base_options.cwd` (the process cwd captured at connect time) via `Path.cwd()`, while `one_shot_dispatch_with_telemetry` in `src/squadron/pipeline/actions/dispatch.py:143-150` reads the same key with `cwd=context.cwd` (the pipeline's working directory). These are two different sources of truth for one config key: a project-level `.squadron.toml` in the pipeline's cwd is honoured on the one-shot path but silently ignored on the session path, so the idle timeout a user configures per project will not apply to the persistent-session dispatch that the timeout exists to bound. The Python rules explicitly forbid "one value, one source" drift here. The session builder (`open_pipeline_session`) should carry the pipeline's cwd into `base_options` (it already sets `cwd=str(Path.cwd())` instead of the run's cwd), or the executor should pass the effective cwd to the session so both paths resolve the key identically.

findings.title: `AgentConfig.auto_memory` defaults to off but the SDK provider now applies the disable variable on every non-opted-in path
findings.description: The provider now always computes `sdk_settings_options(config.setting_sources or [], auto_memory=config.auto_memory, ...)` and always sets `kwargs["env"] = settings["env"]`. Because `AgentConfig.auto_memory` defaults to `False`, every caller that does not explicitly set the flag — including `sq serve` (`src/squadron/server/routes/agents.py:49`, `:179`) and the auth probe (`src/squadron/providers/auth.py:234`) — now gets `CLAUDE_CODE_DISABLE_AUTO_MEMORY=1` injected into the CLI's environment. Previously the disable variable was only applied to the explicit `setting_sources == []` case, so `sq serve` agents kept auto-memory. This is a behaviour change on paths the slice's scope explicitly excludes ("`sq serve` agent spawning ... Neither is an automated pipeline or review path"), and it is not covered by any test. Either the default should stay `True` for non-pipeline callers with the pipeline paths opting in explicitly (the reverse of the current polarity), or the provider should only inject the variable when the caller asked for it — otherwise "auto-memory off" leaks into paths that were never opted into the policy.

findings.title: Session-path `system_prompt` guard rejects a step that declares a prompt but resolved to a non-session profile
findings.description: The new guard in `_dispatch_via_session` fires on `context.params.get("system_prompt")` before the model is resolved, so it is only reached when the session path was chosen. However, the guard is placed *after* the `allowed_tools` guard but *before* `context.resolver.resolve(...)` — so a step that declares `system_prompt` and resolves to an SDK pool alias that is not the session path never reaches this code, while a step that resolves to the session path is rejected even when the step's `system_prompt` would have been appended to the preset by the one-shot path. The design (D8) calls for the session path to reject a step `system_prompt`, so the intent is right, but the check keys on the raw param being truthy rather than on the resolved behaviour: an empty-string `system_prompt: ""` passes the guard (falsy) while a whitespace-only `" "` is rejected, and a step-level `system_prompt` that was already merged into `merged_action_params` for other steps is not distinguished from one the step itself declared. Consider keying the guard on the resolved prompt being non-empty after normalisation, so the error matches the actual condition ("the step's system prompt would be ignored").

findings.title: `sdk_turns.DispatchTurns.collect` marks progress before the rate-limit rejection check can reset it
findings.description: `_read_turn` inspects a `RateLimitEvent` with `event_blocks(...)` *before* calling `turns.collect(...)`, so a rejected event correctly does not set `progressed`. The ordering here is right and matches the original comment. Recording this so the invariant is not broken by a later refactor: `turns.progressed` is set inside `collect()` and also explicitly set to `True` on the `is_error` result path, and `_read_turn_with_retry` resets it at the top of each attempt — the retry budget therefore bounds consecutive failures only, which is the documented intent.

findings.title: The bool config coercion accepts a wide spelling set with no single source of truth
findings.description: `_coerce_bool` accepts `true/yes/on/1` and `false/no/off/0`, case-insensitively, and reports the accepted set in the error message. The spellings live in one place (`_TRUE_SPELLINGS` / `_FALSE_SPELLINGS`), which satisfies the "never scatter comparison values" rule. The set is broader than TOML's own `true/false`, but the lenient parsing is deliberate and documented, and the CLI surfaces the accepted set on failure. No action required.

findings.title: `_display_value` centralises the bool rendering used by both `config get` and `config list`
findings.description: The new helper is the single place that renders a resolved config value, so the TOML spelling for bools (`true`/`false`) cannot drift between the two commands. `config set` now also catches `ValueError` alongside `KeyError`, so an invalid bool spelling exits 1 with the message rather than surfacing a traceback. The `config set` success line still echoes the raw user input (`Set pipeline.auto_memory = maybe`) rather than the coerced value — minor, but it means the confirmation can differ from what was written for the non-canonical spellings (`yes`, `on`, `1`).
